invocation: import sys, os, importlib; sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(sys.argv[1])))); sys.argv = ['lib.security', 'gate', 'flow_finish', '--path', sys.argv[2]]; importlib.import_module('lib.security.cli').run()
limits: Covers the lib.security gate's OWN discrimination on a single planted CRITICAL secret (a synthetic AWS access key id) - not every scanner module scan_quick runs, and not flow_deploy's separate, stricter policy. The invocation imports lib.security.cli by its real dotted name rather than running {gate} as a top-level script, because cli.py uses package-relative imports (from .config import ...) that fail outside package context; sys.path is seeded from {gate}'s own path so the anchor substitution (control.json's whole mechanism) actually swaps which lib/security/cli.py gets imported, rather than always importing the real one regardless of {gate}. The anchor's lib/security/__init__.py is load-bearing, not boilerplate: without it, lib (a namespace package, no __init__.py anywhere) merges the anchor's and the real tree's lib/security/ portions, and Python's import system still finds the real one's __init__.py and resolves lib.security.cli to the REAL file even with the anchor's directory first on sys.path - the anchor silently never ran, and the control read as INERT instead of PASS (measured while building this control). A regular package with its own __init__.py in the FIRST sys.path entry wins outright instead of merging.

anchors.origin: a minimal always-PASS stand-in written for this control (#1394) - lib.security's own gate has no earlier, simpler implementation to borrow a historical blind version from
